scenes.kicker: F01 · Introduction to Financial Accounting · Module 4
scenes.head: The complete accounting cycle
scenes.sub: Every period, every business runs the same nine steps, from analysing a transaction to proving that the ledger is ready for the next period. See the whole cycle at once, use the optional worksheet and reversing entries, correct errors after posting, and protect the records with internal control.

segs.say: The complete accounting cycle. Every period, every business runs the same nine steps, from analysing a transaction to proving that the ledger is ready for the next period. See the whole cycle at once, use the optional worksheet and reversing entries, correct errors after posting, and protect the records with internal control.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: List the nine steps of the accounting cycle in order, and say which happen during the period and which at its end.
Record reversing entries for accruals and show that they lead to the same balances as recording without them.
Record correcting entries for errors found after posting: a wrong account, a wrong amount and an omitted entry.
Explain what internal control is, and apply segregation of duties, authorisation, documentation, physical safeguards and reconciliations to a small business.
Apply the whole cycle to a small business, from its first transaction to its post-closing trial balance.
Distinguish the steps that accounting software automates from the judgements it cannot make.

scenes.head: Lantern’s first month is complete.

segs.say: Lantern’s first month is complete. Since 1 March, Ana and her accountant have analysed fifteen transactions, recorded them in the journal, posted them to the ledger, tested the ledger with a trial balance, made seven adjustments, prepared the financial statements, closed the temporary accounts and proved the result with a post-closing trial balance. On 1 April the sequence begins again: the same steps, in the same order.

scenes.head: That sequence is the accounting cycle: the steps a business repeats every accounting period to turn its transactions into financial statements and to…

segs.say: That sequence is the accounting cycle: the steps a business repeats every accounting period to turn its transactions into financial statements and to make its ledger ready for the next period. You have learned each step in its own lesson. This one puts them together, adds the optional tools that support them, and asks what keeps the whole process honest.
Analyse transactions. Decide from the source document whether an event is a transaction, which accounts it affects and by how much (lessons 3 and 5).
Journalise. Record each transaction as a balanced journal entry, in date order (lesson 5).
Post. Transfer each journal line to its account in the general ledger (lesson 6).
Prepare an unadjusted trial balance. List every ledger balance and confirm that debits equal credits (lesson 7).
Adjust. Record and post adjusting entries for deferrals, accruals and depreciation, so that revenue and expenses fall in the right period (lesson 9).
Prepare an adjusted trial balance. The balances after adjustment, and the source for the statements (lesson 9).
Prepare the financial statements. The income statement, statement of changes in equity, balance sheet and statement of cash flows (lesson 10).
Close. Record and post the closing entries (lesson 11).
Prepare a post-closing trial balance. Confirm that only permanent accounts remain and that they balance (lesson 11).
The accounting cycle. Steps 1 to 3 repeat throughout the period; steps 4 to 9 are done once, at its end; then the next period begins.

scenes.head: Steps 1 to 3 happen throughout the period, every time something happens: a sale, a purchase, a payment.

segs.say: Steps 1 to 3 happen throughout the period, every time something happens: a sale, a purchase, a payment. Steps 4 to 9 happen once, at the end of the period, in a burst of work that accountants call the close. Between steps 4 and 7 some accountants use a worksheet, and on the first day of the new period some record reversing entries. Both are optional, and both are explained below; some textbooks, OpenStax among them, count reversing entries as an optional tenth step.
Lantern’s March cycle in figures (fictional)

scenes.head: Each step uses the output of the one before.

segs.say: Each step uses the output of the one before. The statements are prepared from the adjusted trial balance, so adjusting must come first: prepared from the unadjusted balances, Lantern’s income statement would have reported net income of $2,290 instead of $990. Closing empties the revenue and expense accounts, so it must come after the statements: close first, and there is nothing left to report.

scenes.head: The three trial balances are checkpoints, placed where errors are cheapest to find.

segs.say: The three trial balances are checkpoints, placed where errors are cheapest to find. The unadjusted trial balance tests the period’s posting before adjustments are piled on top. The adjusted trial balance tests the adjustments before anything is published. The post-closing trial balance tests the closing before the next period builds on it. An error caught at its own checkpoint is traced through a handful of entries; the same error found months later has to be traced through hundreds.

scenes.head: Three trial balances, three questions

segs.say: Three trial balances, three questions. Unadjusted: did the period’s entries post in balance? Adjusted: are the balances ready to report? Post-closing: is the ledger ready for the next period, with only permanent accounts open? Each answers its question about arithmetic only. None proves that the right accounts and amounts were used.

scenes.head: A worksheet is an internal working paper, today usually a spreadsheet, that lays the end-of-period steps side by side.

segs.say: A worksheet is an internal working paper, today usually a spreadsheet, that lays the end-of-period steps side by side. The traditional ten-column worksheet has a debit and a credit column for each of five stages: the unadjusted trial balance, the adjustments, the adjusted trial balance, the income statement and the balance sheet. Each account’s balance is carried across the page to the statement it belongs on. The worksheet is not a financial statement and is never published, and using one is optional. It helps an accountant plan the adjustments and draft the statements before any adjusting entry is journalised.
Part of a worksheet for Lantern at 31 March, condensed to one column per stage (fictional)

scenes.head: The worksheet also produces net income before any statement is written.

segs.say: The worksheet also produces net income before any statement is written. Across all of Lantern’s accounts, the income statement columns hold $6,110 of debits (the expenses) and $7,100 of credits (the revenue); the difference, $990, is net income. The balance sheet columns differ by the same amount: $43,000 of debits (assets of $42,700 before accumulated depreciation is deducted, plus dividends of $300) against $42,010 of credits (accumulated depreciation, liabilities and common stock). Adding the $990 to the credit side balances them, because the period’s profit is the one change in equity that has not yet reached the balance sheet accounts. Closing is what puts it there.

scenes.head: A reversing entry is made on the first day of a new period and is the exact opposite of an adjusting entry made at the end of the previous one.

segs.say: A reversing entry is made on the first day of a new period and is the exact opposite of an adjusting entry made at the end of the previous one. It is optional and is normally used for accruals (accrued expenses and accrued revenues), which a later payment or receipt will settle. Its purpose is convenience: whoever records that later payment can do it the routine way, without having to know that part of it was accrued last period.

scenes.head: Take Lantern’s accrued wages.

segs.say: Take Lantern’s accrued wages. At 31 March, adjustment a5 recorded $1,400 of wages that the baristas earned on 16–31 March, to be paid on 5 April: debit Wages Expense, credit Wages Payable. Closing then took Wages Expense to zero. There are two ways to record the 5 April payroll, and they end in the same place.
With a reversing entry (fictional)
Without a reversing entry (fictional)

scenes.head: With the reversal, Wages Expense briefly carries a credit balance of $1,400, an unusual balance that disappears when the payroll is recorded.

segs.say: With the reversal, Wages Expense briefly carries a credit balance of $1,400, an unusual balance that disappears when the payroll is recorded. After 5 April both routes show Wages Payable at zero, no April wages expense from this payroll, and cash $1,400 lower. The reversal changes no result; it only lets the payroll be recorded as an ordinary expense.

scenes.head: To see the rest of the month, suppose (hypothetical figures) that on 20 April Lantern pays $1,500 for wages earned on 1–15 April, and that on 30…

segs.say: To see the rest of the month, suppose (hypothetical figures) that on 20 April Lantern pays $1,500 for wages earned on 1–15 April, and that on 30 April it accrues $1,600 for 16–30 April. The table follows the balance of Wages Expense through April by both routes.
Balance of Wages Expense in April, with and without the reversing entry (hypothetical April figures)

scenes.head: Both routes give April wages expense of 1,500 + 1,600 = 3,100, which is what the baristas earned in April.

segs.say: Both routes give April wages expense of 1,500 + 1,600 = 3,100, which is what the baristas earned in April. Reversing entries guard against a specific slip: the payroll clerk who, not knowing about the accrual, records the 5 April payment as Wages Expense when no reversal has been made. April’s wages expense would then be 1,400 + 1,500 + 1,600 = 4,500, and Wages Payable would still include $1,400 that nobody is owed.

scenes.head: Reverse only accruals that a later cash payment or receipt will settle.

segs.say: Reverse only accruals that a later cash payment or receipt will settle. Reversing depreciation, or the expiry of prepaid insurance, would simply cancel a correct adjustment, because no later transaction will record that expense again.

scenes.head: Errors are found at every stage: when a trial balance doesn’t balance, when a reconciliation fails, when a reviewer asks why an account looks odd.

segs.say: Errors are found at every stage: when a trial balance doesn’t balance, when a reconciliation fails, when a reviewer asks why an account looks odd. Once an entry has been posted, it is not erased or overwritten. Instead the accountant records a correcting entry, a new journal entry that brings the accounts to the balances they would have had if the original entry had been right. This preserves the audit trail: anyone can see what was recorded, when it was fixed and why.

scenes.head: One method works for every correction.

segs.say: One method works for every correction. Write the entry that was made, write the entry that should have been made, and record the difference, account by account. Lines that were right in both drop out. Three errors Lantern could have made in March show the patterns. Each is hypothetical, and each is supposed to be found during the review of the unadjusted trial balance, before the adjusting entries.

Wrong account. Suppose the $350 for March advertising (10 March) had been debited to Prepaid Advertising instead of Advertising Expense. Cash was right; only the debit was misplaced. The correction moves it: debit Advertising Expense 350, credit Prepaid Advertising 350. Uncorrected, the error would overstate both assets and net income by $350.

Wrong amount. Suppose the $1,200 rent payment (28 March) had been keyed as $2,100 on both lines. Rent Expense and the cash paid are each $900 too large, so the correction debits Cash 900 and credits Rent Expense 900. The trial balance could not catch this error, because both sides were wrong by the same amount; the bank reconciliation would. Notice that 900 is divisible by 9, the signature of two transposed digits.

Omitted entry. Suppose the $260 utilities bill (31 March) had never been recorded. Nothing needs undoing: the correction is simply the missing entry, debit Utilities Expense 260, credit Accounts Payable 260, with a memo explaining why it is late.
The three corrections, recorded on 31 March (hypothetical errors, fictional case)

scenes.head: If the journal entry was right and only the posting went astray, for example a correct amount posted to the wrong ledger account, a manual system…

segs.say: If the journal entry was right and only the posting went astray, for example a correct amount posted to the wrong ledger account, a manual system fixes the ledger rather than adding a journal entry. In accounting software posting is automatic, so posting errors of that kind don’t arise; errors, and their corrections, are in the entries themselves.

scenes.head: Errors in statements already issued

segs.say: Errors in statements already issued. Correcting entries fix errors found before the statements are issued. An error discovered in financial statements that have already been issued is treated differently. Under IFRS (IAS 8) a material error from a prior period is corrected retrospectively, by restating the comparative figures; US GAAP (ASC 250) likewise corrects material errors in previously issued statements by restating them. The correction does not pass through the current period’s profit. An immaterial error from an earlier period is usually corrected in the current period instead.

scenes.head: The cycle produces reliable numbers only if the entries going into it are genuine, complete and accurate.

segs.say: The cycle produces reliable numbers only if the entries going into it are genuine, complete and accurate. Internal control is the set of processes an organisation uses to make sure that happens, and more broadly to protect its assets, comply with the law and run its operations well. A widely used framework is published by COSO, the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. First issued in 1992 and updated in 2013, it defines internal control in one sentence:

Internal control is a process, effected by an entity’s board of directors, management, and other personnel, designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the achievement of objectives relating to operations, reporting, and compliance. (COSO, Internal Control — Integrated Framework: Executive Summary (May 2013))

scenes.head: Three parts of that definition matter.

segs.say: Three parts of that definition matter. Internal control is a process carried out by people, not a binder of rules on a shelf. It gives reasonable assurance, not a guarantee: two employees who collude, or a manager who overrides a control, can defeat it, and some controls would cost more than the losses they prevent. And it serves three kinds of objective at once: running operations well, reporting reliably and complying with laws and regulations.

scenes.head: COSO organises internal control into five components: the control environment, the tone set by owners and managers and their commitment to integrity…

segs.say: COSO organises internal control into five components: the control environment, the tone set by owners and managers and their commitment to integrity; risk assessment, working out what could go wrong; control activities, the specific checks; information and communication, getting the right information to the right people; and monitoring activities, checking that the controls keep working. The 2013 framework sets out seventeen principles under these five components.

scenes.head: In a small business, the control activities are where the framework becomes concrete:

segs.say: In a small business, the control activities are where the framework becomes concrete:

scenes.head: In a small business, the control activities are where the framework becomes concrete:

segs.say: Segregation of duties. No one person should handle every stage of a transaction: authorising it, recording it and holding the asset involved. If the person who receives customers’ cash also records it and reconciles the bank account, they can take cash and hide the shortfall. Split those tasks and a theft needs two people.
Authorisation. Transactions are approved by someone with the authority to approve them, within set limits: for example, the owner approves every purchase over $500 before it is ordered.
Documentation. Every entry is supported by a source document, and documents such as invoices and receipts are prenumbered, so that a missing one is noticed.
Physical safeguards. Cash, stock and equipment are locked away; computer records are protected by passwords and backed up.

Reconciliations and independent checks. The records are compared with an independent source: the ledger’s cash with the bank statement, Accounts Payable with suppliers’ statements, the Supplies account with a count. Lantern’s supplies adjustment (a2) began with exactly such a count.

scenes.head: Internal control in US public companies

segs.say: Internal control in US public companies. In the United States, section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, through the rules of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), requires each public company’s annual report to include management’s assessment of its internal control over financial reporting. Larger companies (accelerated and large accelerated filers) must also include their auditor’s attestation report on it; the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 exempted smaller companies from the auditor’s part, but not from management’s assessment.

chapters.title: What software automates, and what still needs judgement

scenes.head: Accounting software has absorbed most of the mechanical steps.

segs.say: Accounting software has absorbed most of the mechanical steps. Posting happens the moment an entry is saved, so the journal and ledger cannot disagree. Trial balances and statements are reports, produced on demand. Year-end closing happens automatically. Bank feeds import transactions and suggest how to record them, and recurring entries such as monthly depreciation can be scheduled. What remains is the part that was always the real work: judgement.

Classification. Is a $4,000 overhaul of an oven a repair expense, or an improvement that extends its life and belongs in Equipment? Is a payment to the owner a dividend, a salary or a loan? Software records whatever account it is given.
Estimates. Depreciation needs a useful life and a residual value, and later courses add estimates such as the customers who won’t pay. These are forecasts, made by people and reviewed by auditors.

Cut-off. Which period does a transaction belong to? A breakfast catered on 31 March but invoiced on 2 April is March revenue (Lantern’s a7). Software uses whatever date it is given; choosing the right period is a judgement.

Completeness and existence. Is every transaction in the records, and is every recorded transaction real? A balanced ledger can still leave out a bill or include a payment to a supplier who doesn’t exist. Controls, reconciliations and review answer that question; arithmetic can’t.

scenes.head: To see the whole cycle at once, follow a much smaller business through one month.

segs.say: To see the whole cycle at once, follow a much smaller business through one month. Fetchwell Dog Training Co., a fictional company founded by Marta Silva, runs group puppy courses and private sessions. It starts trading on 1 May 2026 and uses only accounts you already know. Steps 1 to 3 cover its eight transactions in May.
Fetchwell Dog Training Co.: May transactions (fictional)

scenes.head: Step 4: posted to the ledger, the entries give an unadjusted trial balance of $8,860 on each side (first column of the table below).

segs.say: Step 4: posted to the ledger, the entries give an unadjusted trial balance of $8,860 on each side (first column of the table below). Step 5: two facts at 31 May need adjusting entries. The equipment has been used for one month of its 36: 3,600 ÷ 36 = 100. And four of the six puppy classes have been held, so 2,160 × 4 ÷ 6 = 1,440 of the advance payments has been earned.
Fetchwell: adjusting entries at 31 May (fictional)
Fetchwell’s three trial balances at 31 May, each balance on its normal side (fictional)

scenes.head: Steps 6 and 7: the adjusted trial balance totals $8,960, and the statements come straight from it.

segs.say: Steps 6 and 7: the adjusted trial balance totals $8,960, and the statements come straight from it.
Fetchwell Dog Training Co., Income statement for May 2026 (fictional)
Fetchwell Dog Training Co., Statement of changes in equity for May 2026 (fictional)
Fetchwell Dog Training Co., Balance sheet at 31 May 2026 (fictional)

scenes.head: The statement of cash flows (not shown) would explain the $4,160 of cash: $1,960 from operating activities, $3,600 spent on investing and $5,800 from…

segs.say: The statement of cash flows (not shown) would explain the $4,160 of cash: $1,960 from operating activities, $3,600 spent on investing and $5,800 from financing. Operating cash exceeds net income of $1,040 because $720 was collected for classes not yet held, $250 of advertising is unpaid and the $100 of depreciation used no cash, while $150 of revenue is still to be collected: 1,040 + 720 + 250 + 100 − 150 = 1,960. Profit and cash are different measures, as lesson 8 showed.
Fetchwell: closing entries at 31 May (fictional)

scenes.head: Steps 8 and 9: after closing, the post-closing trial balance (last column of the table) lists only permanent accounts and totals $7,910.

segs.say: Steps 8 and 9: after closing, the post-closing trial balance (last column of the table) lists only permanent accounts and totals $7,910. Debits of $7,910 less the $100 of accumulated depreciation equal total assets of $7,810; credits are liabilities of $970 plus equity of $6,840 plus that same $100. Every lesson in this course has played its part: the equation and the debit and credit rules in the entries, the ledger and trial balances, accrual adjustments, the statements, and closing.

scenes.head: Correcting entry

segs.say: Correcting entry: Correcting entry = Correct entry − Entry made.
Correct entry: The entry that should have been recorded ($).
Entry made: The entry that was actually recorded and posted ($).
It assumes this: Work account by account, treating debits as positive and credits as negative. A positive difference is a debit line in the correction, a negative one a credit line.
Accounts that were right in both entries drop out of the correction.

scenes.head: Wages accrued at the end of a period

segs.say: Wages accrued at the end of a period: Accrued wages = Pay for the pay period × (Days worked by the period end)/(Days in the pay period).
Pay for the pay period: The total that will be paid for the whole pay period ($).
Days worked by the period end: Days of the pay period that fall in the period being closed (days).
Days in the pay period: Length of the pay period (days).
It assumes this: Pay builds up evenly over the days of the pay period.
With a reversing entry, the new period’s expense from this payroll is the full payment minus the accrued wages.

chapters.title: Example: Insurance recorded as an expense

scenes.head: Insurance recorded as an expense

segs.say: Loomline Apparel, a fictional clothing brand, pays $2,400 on 1 September 2026 for a 12-month insurance policy on its studio and stock. The bookkeeper debits Insurance Expense and credits Cash. On 30 September, before the adjusting entries, the accountant notices. Record the correction and the September adjustment, and give the two balances that result.

scenes.head: Insurance recorded as an expense

segs.say: Step 1. Entry made: debit Insurance Expense 2,400, credit Cash 2,400.
Step 2. Entry that should have been made: debit Prepaid Insurance 2,400, credit Cash 2,400, because the payment buys cover for twelve months and is an asset until it is used.
Step 3. The difference: Cash is the same in both and drops out. Prepaid Insurance needs a debit of 2,400 and Insurance Expense a credit of 2,400. That is the correcting entry.
Step 4. Now adjust as usual: one month has expired, 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200. Debit Insurance Expense 200, credit Prepaid Insurance 200.

Step 5. Balances at 30 September: Prepaid Insurance 2,400 − 200 = 2,200; Insurance Expense 2,400 − 2,400 + 200 = 200. A single entry, debit Prepaid Insurance 2,200 and credit Insurance Expense 2,200, would reach the same balances in one step.

scenes.head: Insurance recorded as an expense

segs.say: Correcting entry: debit Prepaid Insurance $2,400, credit Insurance Expense $2,400; then the adjustment of $200. Prepaid Insurance is $2,200 and Insurance Expense $200 at 30 September.

Uncorrected, the error would have understated September’s profit by $2,200 and left the balance sheet without an asset of $2,200, and the next eleven months would have shown no insurance expense at all. One misclassified entry distorts twelve months of results.

chapters.title: Example: A pay period that straddles the year end

scenes.head: A pay period that straddles the year end

segs.say: The Saltmarsh Inn, a fictional hotel, pays its staff every two weeks. The pay period running from 28 December 2026 to 10 January 2027 (14 days) costs $9,800 and is paid on 15 January 2027. The hotel closes its books on 31 December. Record the year-end accrual, then compare recording the payment with and without a reversing entry. How much of this payroll is January’s expense?

scenes.head: A pay period that straddles the year end

segs.say: Step 1. Pay per day: 9,800 ÷ 14 = 700. Four days (28–31 December) fall in 2026, so the accrual at 31 December is 700 × 4 = 2,800: debit Wages Expense, credit Wages Payable. Closing carries this 2,800 into 2026’s profit.

Step 2. With a reversal: on 1 January debit Wages Payable 2,800 and credit Wages Expense 2,800, which leaves Wages Expense with a credit balance of 2,800. On 15 January the payroll clerk records the whole 9,800 as Wages Expense. January’s expense from this payroll is 9,800 − 2,800 = 7,000.

Step 3. Without a reversal: on 15 January the entry must split the payment, debiting Wages Payable 2,800 (settling the accrual) and Wages Expense 7,000. January’s expense is again 7,000, and Wages Payable is zero by both routes.
Step 4. Check against the days: 10 days (1–10 January) fall in 2027, and 10 × 700 = 7,000.
Step 5. The risk the reversal removes: a clerk who records the whole 9,800 as expense without a reversal would overstate January’s wages by 2,800 and leave 2,800 in Wages Payable that nobody is owed.

scenes.head: A pay period that straddles the year end

segs.say: January bears $7,000 of this payroll by either route, and Wages Payable returns to zero. The reversing entry lets the full $9,800 be recorded as a routine expense.

A hotel with a fortnightly payroll has a pay period straddling almost every year end. The accountant makes the accrual and its reversal centrally, once a year, so that the payroll team can record every payment the same way and never needs to know which ones were partly accrued.

chapters.title: Example: Two errors found before the year-end close

scenes.head: Two errors found before the year-end close

segs.say: Ridgeway Home Batteries, a fictional company that installs home battery-storage systems, closes its year on 31 December 2026. Before closing, its finance lead reviews the adjusted trial balance and finds two problems. First, a $6,500 battery-testing rig bought for cash on 1 October was recorded as Repairs Expense; it should last five years, with no residual value. Second, on 1 December the company accepted an $18,000 note receivable at 6% a year from a commercial customer, with interest due when the note matures, and no interest has been accrued. Record the corrections, find the effect on net income, and decide whether they should be made before or after closing.

scenes.head: Two errors found before the year-end close

segs.say: Step 1. Wrong account. Made: debit Repairs Expense 6,500, credit Cash 6,500. Correct: debit Equipment 6,500, credit Cash 6,500. Difference: debit Equipment 6,500, credit Repairs Expense 6,500.

Step 2. Once the rig is recognised as equipment it must be depreciated from 1 October: 6,500 ÷ 5 = 1,300 a year, and for three months 1,300 × 3 ÷ 12 = 325. Debit Depreciation Expense 325, credit Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment 325.
Step 3. Omitted accrual. December’s interest is 18,000 × 6% × 1 ÷ 12 = 90. Debit Interest Receivable 90, credit Interest Revenue 90.
Step 4. Effect on net income: expenses fall by 6,500 and rise by 325, and revenue rises by 90, so net income rises by 6,500 − 325 + 90 = 6,265. Total assets rise by the same amount.

Step 5. Timing: before closing. The corrections change 2026 revenue and expense accounts, which must still be open; posted after closing, they would land in 2027. And once the statements are issued, a material error would have to be corrected by restating them.

scenes.head: Two errors found before the year-end close

segs.say: Three entries: debit Equipment $6,500 and credit Repairs Expense $6,500; debit Depreciation Expense $325 and credit Accumulated Depreciation—Equipment $325; debit Interest Receivable $90 and credit Interest Revenue $90. Net income rises by $6,265. Make them before closing.

Neither error could be caught by software or by a trial balance: the rig was recorded in the account the user chose, and nothing prompted the accrual. The review was the control that found them. Ridgeway might add a rule as well: any purchase above a set amount is classified by the accountant, not by the person who buys it.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: A mixed set from Lantern’s March: five transactions and four adjustments. For each one, choose the accounts, the direction and side of each change, the amounts, the effect on the equation and the statements affected. The mix is the point: in real life nobody tells you which kind of entry comes next. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Run Fetchwell’s whole month through the ledger: eight transactions, two adjustments and four closing entries. Before each balance is revealed, work it out yourself, and watch the trial balance move from $8,860 to $8,960 to $7,910. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “The trial balance balances, so the books are right.”

segs.say: “The trial balance balances, so the books are right.”. A trial balance tests arithmetic only. Lantern’s rent keyed as $2,100 on both lines, advertising debited to the wrong account and a bill never recorded all leave it in balance. Reconciliations, source documents and review find these errors; the trial balance can’t.

scenes.head: “Reversing entries change the next period’s results.”

segs.say: “Reversing entries change the next period’s results.”. They change only how the later payment is recorded. With or without the reversal, Lantern’s April wages expense is $3,100 and Wages Payable at 30 April is $1,600. A reversing entry is optional; what it removes is the need for the payroll clerk to know about the accrual.

scenes.head: “Any adjustment can be reversed.”

segs.say: “Any adjustment can be reversed.”. Reverse only accruals that a later payment or receipt will settle. Reversing depreciation or the expiry of prepaid insurance would cancel a correct expense, because no later transaction will record it again.

scenes.head: “Fix a mistake by deleting the entry.”

segs.say: “Fix a mistake by deleting the entry.”. In a manual journal, a posted entry is never erased: the correction is a new, dated entry with a memo, so the audit trail shows what happened. Software may let you edit an entry in an open period, but it keeps a history of the change, and a locked period should be corrected only by a documented correcting entry.

scenes.head: “Internal control is about catching thieves.”

segs.say: “Internal control is about catching thieves.”. Fraud is one risk, but most of what controls catch is honest error: a transposed figure, a bill entered twice, an expense coded to the wrong account. Controls aim at reliable reporting and well-run operations as well as safe assets, and they give reasonable assurance, not certainty. A three-person business can’t separate every duty, so it relies more on the owner’s review.

scenes.head: “The software does the accounting.”

segs.say: “The software does the accounting.”. Software posts, totals, reports and closes. It doesn’t decide whether a purchase is equipment or an expense, how long equipment will last, which period a sale belongs to, or whether a supplier is real. Those judgements are the accountant’s, and errors in them pass straight through a perfectly balanced ledger.

scenes.head: On 1 April, Ana’s accountant opens the new period from the post-closing trial balance: thirteen permanent balances, with every revenue, expense and…

segs.say: On 1 April, Ana’s accountant opens the new period from the post-closing trial balance: thirteen permanent balances, with every revenue, expense and dividend account at zero. Lantern doesn’t use reversing entries: on 5 April it will debit Wages Payable, and on 2 April the Pier Nine invoice records nothing new, as lesson 9 showed. But suppose that before the first April transaction the accountant considered reversing March’s accruals. Two of them will be settled by ordinary April transactions: the wages (a5), paid on 5 April, and the Pier Nine breakfast (a7), invoiced on 2 April. Reversing a7 would mean crediting Accounts Receivable and debiting Catering Revenue for $600 on 1 April, so that the invoice could be recorded as a normal credit sale on 2 April. If Ana took on a part-time bookkeeper who didn’t know March’s history, reversing both would be the safer choice.

scenes.head: Suppose that, as Lantern grows, Ana does hire the bookkeeper.

segs.say: Suppose that, as Lantern grows, Ana does hire the bookkeeper. For the first time someone other than her will record transactions. With three people, full segregation of duties is impossible, so she designs controls that fit the business: each task goes to someone who can do it without also being able to hide a mistake or a theft in it.
A division of duties for Lantern (fictional)

scenes.head: No arrangement is foolproof.

segs.say: No arrangement is foolproof. Ana herself both approves payments and reconciles the bank, so the check on the owner is the external accountant’s review at year end. The aim is reasonable assurance at a sensible cost, which is exactly what COSO’s definition asks for. The controls also make the bookkeeper’s work easier to trust, which matters when a lender asks to see the statements.

scenes.head: This course has kept Lantern’s books for its catering and workshops, which are services: they hold no inventory, and the statements fit on a page.

segs.say: This course has kept Lantern’s books for its catering and workshops, which are services: they hold no inventory, and the statements fit on a page. Lantern’s online shop sells bags of coffee beans, and those need accounts for stock and for the cost of the goods it sells. F02, Financial Statement Preparation, builds on the cycle you now know: the four statements in depth and how they connect, inventory and the cost of goods sold, depreciation methods beyond straight-line, receivables and payables, working capital, and the differences between US GAAP and IFRS.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: The accounting cycle has nine steps: analyse, journalise, post, unadjusted trial balance, adjust, adjusted trial balance, statements, close, post-closing trial balance. Steps 1–3 happen throughout the period; steps 4–9 at its end.
The order matters: statements come from adjusted balances, and closing comes after the statements. Each trial balance is a checkpoint on arithmetic, not on correctness.
A worksheet is an optional working paper that carries each balance from the trial balance to the statements; its income statement columns differ by net income.

A reversing entry, made on the first day of a new period, is the exact opposite of an accrual adjustment. It is optional, changes no result, and lets the later payment or receipt be recorded the routine way.

A correcting entry is the difference between the entry that should have been made and the entry that was made. Posted entries are never erased; errors in statements already issued are corrected by restatement.

Internal control is a process giving reasonable assurance about operations, reporting and compliance. COSO’s five components are the control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.
Key control activities: segregation of duties, authorisation, documentation, physical safeguards, and reconciliations and independent checks.
Software automates posting, trial balances, statements and closing; classification, estimates, cut-off and completeness still need judgement.
